level.title: Flying level around a ball
level.mini: An airliner holding its altitude follows the curve: its nose turns against the stars by {{rateMin}} per minute, far too little to feel. Locked to the stars instead, it would be climbing away from the surface at {{climb10}} within ten minutes.
level.text: Two airliners at {{kmh}}. The teal one holds its altitude, as every airliner does: the altimeter reads air pressure, and a surface of constant pressure follows the Earth. Its attitude indicator, pulled towards the plumb line by gravity [1], stays level while its nose turns against the fixed stars by the arc flown: {{rateMin}} per minute, {{rateHour}} per hour. The grey one keeps its nose fixed against the stars: it leaves along a straight line, {{rise1}} too high after one minute, and its own attitude indicator shows the nose rising. On the left, a stone swung on a rope: the rope pulls it round, and the grey stone, rope cut, goes straight on, as the grey aircraft does. For the aircraft the rope is gravity (amber). The Earth is drawn smaller than the altitude, at uniform scale, with the factor printed; the numbers are the real ones.
level.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: an airliner holding its altitude for thousands of kilometres with its nose fixed against the stars.
fx-level.title: Why pilots never feel the nose go down
fx-level.mini: Over an arc d, the local vertical turns by d/(R + h). At {{kmh}} that is {{rateMin}} per minute. A nose locked to the stars would follow the tangent and end Δh ≈ d²/2(R + h) too high.
fx-level.text: An aircraft flying an arc d around a sphere of radius R, at altitude h, sees its local vertical turn by the angle θ = d/(R + h) at the centre. To stay level its nose must turn by the same angle against the stars, at the rate ω = v/(R + h): {{rateMin}} per minute at {{kmh}}. The small dot of an attitude indicator stands for about 2° of pitch [1], that is {{dotMin}} minutes of curvature. A nose kept fixed against the stars follows the tangent instead, and rises Δh ≈ d²/2(R + h) above the level path. Level flight also carries a centripetal acceleration v²/(R + h), {{cent}} of g. The drawing is not to scale.
fx-level.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: a local vertical that stays parallel to itself however far the aircraft flies.
eot.title: An aircraft weighs less flying east
eot.mini: Real airborne gravity from NOAA, flown east and west over Lake Erie. Uncorrected, as a flat Earth requires, neighbouring lines of opposite directions disagree by {{gdRms0}}. With the globe's Eötvös correction, by {{gdRms2}}.
eot.text: NOAA's GRAV-D block EN02 was flown at 20,000 ft over Lake Erie in 2011, along east–west lines 10 km apart, alternately eastbound and westbound [1]. Each curve is one line against longitude, blue flown east, purple flown west, reduced to a common height and latitude. An aircraft flying east circles the Earth's axis faster than the ground and needs less lift; flying west, more (Eötvös, 1919 [2]). Without any correction, as a flat Earth requires, neighbouring lines of opposite directions differ by {{gdRms0}}. With the rotation term only, {{gdRms1}}. With the full globe correction, rotation plus v²/R [3], {{gdRms2}}, close to the survey's own crossover residuals. Letting the data choose the radius gives R = {{gdR}}.
eot.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: uncorrected eastbound and westbound lines that agree.
fx-eot.title: The Eötvös correction
fx-eot.mini: Flying east, an aircraft circles the Earth's axis faster than the ground; flying west, slower: Δg = 2Ω·v_E·cos φ + v²/(R + h). At {{kmh}} and 45°N: {{eoE}} east, {{eoW}} west. On a plane: 0.
fx-eot.text: At latitude φ the ground circles the Earth's axis on a circle of radius R cos φ. An aircraft flying east at v_E adds to that motion, one flying west subtracts from it, and following the curved surface costs v²/(R + h) in any direction. Together, the apparent loss of weight per unit mass is Δg = 2Ω·v_E·cos φ + v²/(R + h): the effect Eötvös demonstrated in 1919 [1], the correction every airborne gravity survey applies [2]. For an airliner at {{kmh}} and 45°N: {{eoE}} flying east, {{eoW}} flying west, {{eoN}} flying north (1 mGal = 10⁻⁵ m/s²). On a plane, still or turning about a vertical axis, horizontal motion changes nothing: the correction is 0. The drawing is schematic.
fx-eot.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: airborne gravimeters reading the same whatever the direction of flight.
eot-scale.title: A bathroom scale flown east and west
eot-scale.mini: The same 70 kg passenger reads {{scE}} on the eastbound lines of a real NOAA survey and {{scW}} on the westbound ones: {{scGap}} apart. The globe predicts {{scPred}}; a flat Earth, the same reading both ways.
eot-scale.text: NOAA's GRAV-D block EN02 was flown over Lake Erie in 2011 along east–west lines 10 km apart, alternately eastbound and westbound [1]. Each bar is one line, south to north: how much more (up) or less (down) a 70 kg passenger would weigh than the average of all the lines, from the meter readings reduced to a common height and latitude. Eastbound, the aircraft circles the Earth's axis faster than the ground and weighs less; westbound, more (Eötvös, 1919 [2]). Measured: {{scE}} east, {{scW}} west, {{scGap}} apart. The globe's formula for each line's speed (black ticks) predicts {{scPred}}. A flat Earth, still or turning about a vertical axis, predicts the same reading on every line (orange dashes). The readings are NOAA's published values with the globe's correction added back; since the published eastbound and westbound lines agree, this difference is what the meter actually felt.
eot-scale.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: the same scale reading on the eastbound and the westbound lines.
eot-fit.title: The Earth's rotation and radius from a gravity survey
eot-fit.mini: Leaving both free, NOAA's airborne gravity lines agree best for Ω = {{jfOm}} times the Earth's rotation, one turn in {{jfDay}}, and R = {{jfR}}.
eot-fit.text: Neighbouring lines of NOAA's block EN02, flown in opposite directions [1], only agree once the Eötvös correction is applied [2]. The gap between two lines is linear in the rotation Ω and in 1/R, so one least-squares fit gives both: Ω = {{jfOm}} Ω₀, one turn in {{jfDay}} (sidereal day 23.93 h), and R = {{jfR}}. Uncertainties: each pair of lines left out in turn (jackknife). Each circle is one pair fitted alone; they slide along the trade-off between the two unknowns (correlation {{jfCorr}}), since the rotation term splits the two directions by {{jfTermOm}} and the curvature term adds only {{jfTermR}}. Orange: the rotation term kept on a plane (R = ∞) leaves {{jfFlatRms}} rms against {{jfRms}}. Limit: the readings are NOAA's published values with the globe's correction added back, and the speeds come from WGS84 coordinates; the fit shows how tightly the agreement of the lines pins Ω and R.
eot-fit.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: lines that agree best with no curvature term at all, or with no rotation.
fx-eotfit.title: Two unknowns from one gap
fx-eotfit.mini: The gap between two lines flown in opposite directions is linear in Ω and in 1/R. The rotation splits them by {{jfTermOm}}, the curvature adds {{jfTermR}} through their speed difference.
fx-eotfit.text: Two neighbouring lines, 10 km apart in the same air, one flown east with the wind behind, one west into it [1]. After correction their gap is d = Δm + 2Ω·Δ(v_E cos φ) + Δ(v²)/(R + h), Δm being the gap between the raw meter readings. Ω and R are the values that make the gaps smallest. The rotation term pulls the two directions apart by about {{jfTermOm}}; R acts only through their difference of speed, about {{jfTermR}}. With airspeed a and a steady tailwind w, the east–west gap is 4a(Ω cos φ + w/R): only that combination would show. The wind changes from line to line, and that is what separates Ω from R. The drawing is schematic.
fx-eotfit.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: a gap between directions that no value of Ω and R can close.
dg.title: A heading indicator drifts the way the globe says
dg.labels: Globe|Motionless plane|Plane turning under the sky
dg.mini: Three free gyros set to 000 on aircraft parked facing north. On the globe, Tromsø loses {{dgTosAbs}} per hour, Singapore nothing, Sydney gains {{dgSydAbs}}. The flat models give no drift, or the same drift everywhere.
dg.text: A free heading indicator keeps its direction in space; the FAA warns it can drift by up to 15° per hour and asks pilots to reset it about every 15 minutes [1]. The part of the Earth's rotation that turns it is Ω sin φ: zero at the equator, largest at the poles, of opposite sign in the southern hemisphere [2]. Three indicators set to 000 together, on aircraft parked facing true north: on the globe, Tromsø loses {{dgTosAbs}} in an hour, Singapore almost nothing, Sydney gains {{dgSydAbs}}. On a motionless plane nothing turns: no drift anywhere. On a plane turning once a day under the sky, every gyro turns by the full 15.04° per hour, the same way everywhere. Friction, real in real instruments, is left out.
dg.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: free gyros drifting the same way, by the same amount, north and south of the equator.
gc.title: Every airliner finds north from the Earth's rotation
gc.labels: Globe|Motionless plane|Plane turning under the sky
gc.mini: Parked at the gate, an airliner's inertial unit measures the Earth's rotation: a part towards true north, Ω cos φ, and a vertical part, Ω sin φ. Their ratio is the airport's latitude. A flat Earth leaves no north to find.
gc.text: An airliner's inertial reference system has three ring-laser gyros [1][2]. Parked at the gate before the first flight, it measures the Earth's rotation, 15.04° per hour, parallel to the Earth's axis. At latitude φ that rotation splits into a horizontal part Ω cos φ pointing to true north and a vertical part Ω sin φ [3]. The first gives north without a compass; the ratio gives the latitude: at London, {{gcH51}} north and {{gcV51}} vertical, 51.5°. Alignment takes 5 minutes at the equator and 10 at 70°, longer up to 82.5°, where the horizontal part becomes too small [1]. On a motionless plane there is no rotation to measure; on a plane turning under the sky the rotation is vertical everywhere: no north, and the same “latitude”, 90°, at every airport.
gc.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: inertial units failing to find north, or reporting the same latitude at every airport.
fx-gyro.title: How a gyro at rest finds north and its latitude
fx-gyro.mini: The Earth's rotation Ω is parallel to its axis. At an airport of latitude φ it splits into Ω cos φ, towards true north, and Ω sin φ, vertical. Their ratio gives φ; the vertical part flips sign at the equator.
fx-gyro.text: A gyroscope keeps its direction in space, so on the rotating Earth it senses the rotation Ω = 15.04° per hour, parallel to the axis. At an airport of latitude φ that vector splits into two parts: Ω cos φ along the ground, pointing to true north, and Ω sin φ along the local vertical [1]. The horizontal part tells an inertial unit where north is; the ratio of the two, tan φ, gives the latitude. The vertical part is what makes a free heading indicator drift, by −Ω sin φ; south of the equator it points down and the drift reverses [2]. The drawing is schematic.
fx-gyro.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: gyros at rest sensing no rotation, or the same vertical rotation at every airport.
schuler.title: A globe inertial unit flown over a plane
schuler.mini: Inertial units turn their level by v/R to follow the curve. Over a plane, that would make the computed position swing around the departure airport: {{schErr}} out after one hour, against 3.7 km allowed.
schuler.text: An inertial unit integrates its accelerations, and to keep “down” pointing down it turns its own level by v/R as it travels [1]. Real units do, and their errors then oscillate with the Schuler period, 2π√(R/g) = {{schuler}}, instead of growing [1][2]; the regulation allows 2 nautical miles per hour on flights up to ten hours [3]. Here the same unit is carried straight over a plane at {{kmh}}: it keeps tilting its level for a curve that is not there, gravity leaks into its horizontal accelerations, and its computed position (orange ring) swings within ±{{schAmp}} of the departure airport. After one hour it is {{schErr}} out. Computed from the unit's equations: there is no plane to fly over.
schuler.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: certified inertial units navigating correctly with no Earth radius in their equations.
fx-schuler.title: A pendulum as long as the Earth's radius
fx-schuler.mini: A pendulum hung from an aircraft down to the Earth's centre would always point down. Its period, 2π√(R/g) = {{schuler}}, is the period of every inertial unit's errors (Schuler, 1923).
fx-schuler.text: Maximilian Schuler showed in 1923 that an instrument which must keep pointing down on a moving vehicle behaves like a pendulum as long as the Earth's radius, hung from the vehicle down to the centre [1]. Such a pendulum stays vertical whatever the vehicle's accelerations, and swings with the period T = 2π√(R/g) = {{schuler}}, that of a satellite skimming the surface [2]. Inertial units are built this way, so their errors oscillate with that period instead of growing. Carried over a plane, the same unit would compute a position x_c = (v/ω_s)·sin(ω_s t), with ω_s = √(g/R): a swing around the departure point, while the true position runs away as v·t. The drawing shows shapes only.
fx-schuler.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: inertial errors that do not oscillate with the {{schuler}} Schuler period.
gjt.title: EI-GJT: when an inertial unit lost its place
gjt.mini: 9 October 2018: a faulty accelerometer sent a Boeing 737's inertial position racing past the North Pole, and the captain's attitude display tilted with it, towards 90°. The unit draws the horizon of where it thinks it is.
gjt.text: Between Porto and Edinburgh, one accelerometer of a Boeing 737-800's left inertial unit failed, reporting about 1.6 g along the track [1]. Black: where the aircraft was, flying north at about 240 m/s. Orange: where the unit placed it, from the groundspeeds the AAIB published, along the same great circle. Because the unit's position on the Earth is used to generate the attitude indication [1], the captain's pitch display rose to 90° over about twenty minutes. The angle between the two positions, seen from the Earth's centre, reaches {{gjt59}} when the attitude is declared invalid: a horizon tilted by that much. The track is schematic, and the groundspeeds were read by eye.
gjt.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: a wrong inertial position leaving the attitude display untouched, since on a plane “down” is the same everywhere.
fx-gjt.title: A wrong position tilts the horizon
fx-gjt.mini: An inertial unit draws the horizon tangent to the Earth where it thinks it is. If that place is Δσ away, measured at the Earth's centre, the horizon shown is tilted by Δσ. On a plane it would not tilt at all.
fx-gjt.text: On a sphere the horizon at a point is the plane tangent to the surface there, and two points separated by the angle Δσ at the Earth's centre have horizons tilted by Δσ from each other. An inertial unit that has lost its place draws the horizon of the wrong point. For EI-GJT, on 9 October 2018, adding up the difference between the faulty unit's groundspeed and the true one, Δσ = Σ(v_IRS − v)·Δt / R, gives {{gjt53}} near the pole and {{gjt59}} when the attitude was declared invalid, close to the 90° pitch the report states [1]. On a plane every point shares the same “down”, and a position error tilts nothing. The drawing is schematic.
fx-gjt.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: attitude displays unaffected by errors in the inertial position.
race.title: Sydney to Santiago: same flight, two maps
race.labels: Sydney – Santiago, globe and flat map
race.mini: The same measured flight time on the globe and on the flat-earth map. On the globe the aircraft flies at {{sydVg}}, near its filed cruise speed. On the flat map it would need {{sydVf}}.
race.text: Sydney–Santiago, airborne {{sydH}} one way and {{sydH2}} the other in FlightAware's records [1]. Left, the globe: the great circle, {{sydKm}}, dips into the Southern Ocean, and the waypoints of the filed flight plan follow it. Right, the usual flat map, the azimuthal-equidistant disc centred on the North Pole [2]: the straight line is {{sydFlat}} and crosses the North Pacific. Both aircraft take off and land together, because the time is the one measured. The globe's aircraft flies at {{sydVg}}, like the filed cruise speed; the disc's would need {{sydVf}}, both ways.
race.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: southern routes whose measured times fit the flat map's longer distances at airliner speeds.
omo.title: Around the world over both poles
omo.labels: One More Orbit, 2019, globe and flat map
omo.mini: In July 2019 a Gulfstream flew around the world over both poles in 46 h 40 min. On the globe the legs add up to {{omoG}}. On the flat map, even touching the most favourable point of the rim: {{omoF}}.
omo.text: On 9–11 July 2019 a Gulfstream G650ER flew from the Kennedy Space Center over the North Pole to Nur-Sultan, to Mauritius, over the South Pole to Punta Arenas and back, in 46 h 39 min 38 s by the FAI's timing [1]: {{omoKm}} at an average of {{omoAvg}}, fuel stops included [2]. Left: the same legs on the globe, {{omoG}}. Right: on the flat disc the South Pole is the whole rim; letting the flat model choose the most favourable point to touch, the trip becomes {{omoF}}, an average of {{omoFv}} including three fuel stops, from an aircraft whose published average was {{omoAvg}}.
omo.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: a flight over both poles taking the time the flat map's distances need.
fx-dist.title: Two ways to measure a flight
fx-dist.mini: The globe measures an arc: d = R·θ. The flat-earth disc measures a chord from the North Pole: d² = r₁² + r₂² − 2r₁r₂ cos Δλ. Same airports, same coordinates; on long southern routes the chord is about twice as long.
fx-dist.text: Give two airports by their latitude φ and longitude λ. On the globe the distance is the arc d = R·θ, where the angle at the Earth's centre θ follows from cos θ = sin φ₁ sin φ₂ + cos φ₁ cos φ₂ cos Δλ. On the usual flat map, the azimuthal-equidistant disc centred on the North Pole [1], each airport sits at r = R(90° − φ) from the centre, and the distance is the chord d² = r₁² + r₂² − 2r₁r₂ cos Δλ. The two agree near the pole and part ways in the south, where the disc stretches everything east–west. Flight times decide: with t = t₀ + d/v, {{nFlights}} real flights on {{nRoutes}} routes fit the globe's arcs to {{rmsGlobe}} [2]. The drawing is schematic.
fx-dist.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: flight times proportional to the chords of the disc rather than to the arcs of the globe.
springs.title: The best flat map anyone could draw
springs.mini: Airports free to slide anywhere on a plane, each route a spring cut to its measured flight time. The best arrangement still misses by {{rmsFlat}}, {{flatRatio}} times the globe, which has no free parameter.
springs.text: Forget every map. Put the {{nAirports}} airports of {{nRoutes}} timed routes anywhere on a plane, and cut each route as a spring to the distance its airborne time allows [1]. The airports slide until the springs are as relaxed as they can get: {{flatDof}} free numbers. They never all go slack: orange springs are stretched beyond what their flights allow, blue ones squeezed. The best arrangement found, the same from every start tried, misses by {{rmsFlat}}; the globe, with every airport at its surveyed coordinates, fits the same times to {{rmsGlobe}}. Beside the springs, each route's length on that plane and on the globe is set against the distance its flight time allows: the globe's points lie on the diagonal, the plane's scatter around it. A sphere's distances cannot be laid flat without stretching some of them.
springs.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: a flat arrangement of the airports that fits the flight times as well as the globe does.
fx-springs.title: Four cities no flat map can hold
fx-springs.mini: On a sphere, four cities can all be {{tetraKm}} apart. On a plane, four points can never all be equally far apart: with three at the corners of a triangle, the fourth is too close to all of them.
fx-springs.text: Place four points on a sphere at the corners of a regular tetrahedron: all six distances are equal, {{tetraKm}} on the Earth. No plane can do that. With three points at the corners of an equilateral triangle, the fourth, in the middle, sits at 58% of the side from each corner; anywhere else, the six distances are even less equal. A network of air routes holds many such constraints at once. That is what the best flat fit runs into: each route is a spring cut to its flight time, the airports slide freely, and the minimum of Σ((|xᵢ − xⱼ| − δᵢⱼ)/δᵢⱼ)² still leaves {{rmsFlat}} of misfit [1]. The drawing is schematic.
fx-springs.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: sets of cities whose measured distances all lie flat on a plane without stretching.
radius.title: The Earth's radius from airline timetables
radius.mini: Each dot: the Earth's radius implied by one route's round-trip flight time and the true airspeed filed in its flight plan. Together: R = {{rfR}} ± {{rfSe}}, {{rfPct}} above the mean radius, as detours and winds predict.
radius.text: Flight times alone give a speed, not a size. But the cruise speed filed in each flight plan is a true airspeed, measured through the air, independent of the ground's shape [1]. On the globe, airborne time = t₀ + R·θ ÷ airspeed, θ being the angle between the two airports at the Earth's centre. Each dot is the radius one route implies, against the route's length; the fit over all {{rfN}} routes gives R = {{rfR}} ± {{rfSe}}, {{rfPct}} above the mean radius of 6,371 km (dashed). High, as it should be: detours from the great circle, winds that never fully cancel and crosswinds all make the Earth look bigger.
radius.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: radii disagreeing from route to route, the southern ones coming out about twice as large.
fx-radius.title: Measuring the Earth with a stopwatch
fx-radius.mini: On a globe, flight time = t₀ + R·θ / airspeed. With the true airspeeds filed in flight plans, airline times give R. Winds never quite cancel: the round-trip mean is (d/v)/(1 − w²/v²), longer than with no wind.
fx-radius.text: An aircraft covers the arc R·θ between two airports at its true airspeed v, θ being their angle at the Earth's centre, fixed by their coordinates. So the airborne time is t = t₀ + R·θ/v, and with v known from the flight plan a stopwatch measures R [1]. The wind is the main trap: out with a tailwind at v + w and back into a headwind at v − w, the mean time is (d/v)·1/(1 − w²/v²), always longer than with no wind, by about 1% for a 100 km/h wind. That bias, like every detour, makes the Earth look bigger: the {{rfN}} routes give R = {{rfR}}, {{rfPct}} above the mean radius. The drawing is schematic.
fx-radius.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: flight times that no single radius can fit.
fx-rope.title: Gravity is the rope
fx-rope.mini: A stone swung on a rope goes round because the rope pulls it inwards. For an airliner the rope is gravity, and only {{cent}} of it is needed to bend the path round the Earth.
fx-rope.text: A stone of mass m swung at speed v on a rope of length r goes round because the rope pulls it towards the hand, with T = m v²/r; cut the rope and it leaves in a straight line. An airliner at altitude h does the same around the Earth, and gravity is the rope. Gravity pulls with m g, the wings push up with the lift L, and the difference, m v²/(R + h), bends the path. At {{kmh}} that is {{cent}} of g: the wings hold up the rest, and the aircraft weighs that much less than on the ground. The pilot never has to push the nose down; the attitude indicator itself is kept level by gravity [1].
fx-rope.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: an airliner in level flight whose weight does not depend on its speed.
fx-world.title: The further south, the longer a parallel on the flat map
fx-world.mini: On the globe a parallel measures 2πR cos φ; on the flat disc, 2πR(π/2 − φ). Equal only at the North Pole: the disc stretches 45°N by {{par45}}, the equator by {{par0}}, 35°S by {{par35}}.
fx-world.text: On the globe, the parallel of latitude φ is a circle of radius R cos φ around the axis. On the usual flat map, the azimuthal-equidistant disc centred on the North Pole [1], it is a circle of radius R(π/2 − φ) around the centre, because distances along the meridians are kept true. The two lengths agree only at the pole. The disc stretches the parallel of 45°N by {{par45}}, the equator by {{par0}}, and 35°S, the latitude of Sydney, Santiago and Cape Town, by {{par35}}. North to south, the globe's meridian crosses a second pole; on the disc the South Pole is the whole rim.
fx-world.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: flights around the southern hemisphere that take the time the disc's much longer parallels need.
world.title: Around the southern hemisphere on scheduled flights
world.labels: Sydney → Santiago → São Paulo → Johannesburg → Perth → Sydney
world.mini: Five scheduled flights circle the southern hemisphere in {{swH}} in the air. On the globe that is {{swVg}}, an airliner's speed. On the flat map it would take {{swVf}}.
world.text: Sydney → Santiago → São Paulo → Johannesburg → Perth → Sydney: five scheduled flights, {{swN}} of them timed by FlightAware [1], {{swH}} in the air, mean of the two directions. On the globe the ring measures {{swG}}: {{swVg}}, like any airliner. On the usual flat map, the azimuthal-equidistant disc [2], the same parallels are far longer the further south they lie, and the ring measures {{swF}}: {{swVf}}, about twice the speed of the aircraft that fly it. Both aircraft take off and land together, because the times are the measured ones.
world.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: a southern ring of flights taking the time the flat map's lengths need.
af1995.title: Concorde around the world: a northern loop that settles nothing
af1995.labels: Concorde AF1995, 15–16 August 1995, globe and flat map
af1995.mini: In 1995 a Concorde flew around the world eastbound in {{afH}}, mostly in the northern hemisphere. On the globe the legs add up to {{afG}}, on the flat map {{afF}}: both within Concorde's speed. This trip does not tell the two apart.
af1995.text: On 15–16 August 1995 an Air France Concorde flew from New York eastbound via Toulouse, Dubai, Bangkok, Guam, Honolulu and Acapulco back to New York in 31 h 27 min 49 s, stops included, over a published {{afPub}} [1]. On the globe the great-circle legs add up to {{afG}}, an average of {{afVg}}. On the flat disc, where the northern parallels are only a little stretched, the same legs measure {{afF}}, {{afX}} more: an average of {{afVf}}, still below Concorde's cruise speed of about {{afVmax}} [2]. A loop that stays mostly north of the equator fits both maps; only flights far into the southern hemisphere, or over both poles, separate them [3].
af1995.verdict: Neither model is favoured: the flat map's distances stay within the aircraft's speed on this northern loop.
pa50.title: Pan Am 50: around the world over both poles
pa50.mini: In 1977 a Boeing 747SP flew around the world over both poles in 54 h 7 min. On the globe its legs add up to {{paG}}, within {{paDiff}} of the FAI's figure. On the flat map: {{paF}}, an average of {{paVf}}.
pa50.text: Pan Am Flight 50, a Boeing 747SP, flew San Francisco → North Pole → London → Cape Town → South Pole → Auckland → San Francisco on 28–30 October 1977, in 54 h 7 min 12 s at 784.31 km/h by the FAI [1][2], {{paPub}}. On the globe, the great-circle legs add up to {{paG}}, {{paDiff}} from that. On the flat disc the South Pole is the whole rim; letting the flat model touch it at the point that suits it best, the trip becomes {{paF}}, an average of {{paVf}} with the three stops included, beyond the 747SP's top speed of Mach 0.92, about 980 km/h [3].
pa50.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: a flight over both poles taking the time the flat map's distances need.
eot-k.title: Testing the correction NOAA injected
eot-k.mini: Keep a fraction k of the globe's Eötvös correction: at k = 0 (flat, still) opposite lines split by {{ekSpread}}; they agree best at k = {{ekStar}}.
eot-k.text: NOAA publishes airborne gravity with the globe's rotation already subtracted (ω and WGS84) [1]. Subtracting a value cannot make lines agree: if it were wrong, eastbound and westbound lines would split by up to {{ekSpread}} rms. No line is adjusted after the fact [1]. Keeping a fraction k of the Eötvös correction [2], neighbouring lines of block EN02 flown in opposite directions [3] agree best at k = {{ekStar}} ({{ekRmsMin}} rms; {{ekRms1}} at k = 1; {{ekRms0}} at k = 0). Limit: speeds come from WGS84 coordinates, so this tests rotation and size together.
eot-k.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: a minimum at 0, or no clear minimum at all.
forces.title: Seen from the aircraft, nothing moves
forces.mini: Two aircraft hold two pressure surfaces, at flight levels 350 and 100. In each one's own frame the forces never change: weight minus lift is only {{fgAc}} and {{fgBc}} of the weight. Only the stars turn above and the ground slides by below.
forces.text: An airliner in level flight holds one air pressure, a surface that follows the Earth: {{fgAp}} at flight level 350, {{fgBp}} at flight level 100 [1]. Its weight points to the centre of the Earth, always straight down for it; lift balances it up to v²/(R + h), {{fgAc}} of the weight at {{fgAv}} and {{fgBc}} at {{fgBv}}; thrust equals air resistance (a lift-to-resistance ratio of {{fgLD}} is assumed). In the aircraft's frame these vectors are the same at every hour; the ground slides by below it and the stars turn above it, the nose turning against them at {{fgAw}} per minute. So the autopilot has nothing to do but hold the pressure. The Earth is drawn smaller than the altitude, at uniform scale.
forces.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: an aircraft that needs a steady correction to stay on its pressure surface.
bearings.title: Which way would the best flat map point you?
bearings.mini: Each route's real heading (the great circle) against the heading the best flat map gives it, step by step: {{bfRms}} rms, {{bfOver90}} headings wrong by more than 90°.
bearings.text: The best flat map was fitted to flight times only, so it is free to point routes anywhere. Lay it on a compass as favourably as possible and compare, for each route, the real heading at the first airport (outer ring, the great circle, nothing fitted) with the heading the map gives it as the fit proceeds (inner ring). A radial line means they agree. At the end the headings differ by {{bfRms}} rms and {{bfOver90}} by more than 90°. Two striking cases (real → map): {{bfEx1}}, {{bfEx1d}} off; {{bfEx2}}, {{bfEx2d}} off. A compass and a heading indicator do measure headings [1].
bearings.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: a flat arrangement whose route headings stay within a few degrees of the real ones while its distances fit the flight times.
mesh.title: Does a shape come out of the flight times alone?
mesh.mini: {{routes}} round trips, no coordinate and no distance: airports laid one by one on a plane stall at {{planeBest}}; on a sphere of free size they settle at {{ss}}, R = {{km}} with the filed airspeed.
mesh.text: Only the airborne times of {{routes}} round trips, both directions averaged, and one rule for every route: time = climb and descent + length, the length in hours of flight [1]. The {{airports}} airports are laid one by one, the best-connected first, each where its times put it. On a plane they stall at {{planeBest}} rms. The same steps on a sphere whose radius is free (a huge sphere is the plane again) settle at {{ss}}, {{ratio}} times better with one number more, and choose R = {{R}} hours of flight; at the true airspeed the airlines file, {{tas}}, R = {{km}}. Only then the real map: turned onto it, the {{fixedN}} airports whose place the times fix sit {{vs}} rms from their real place. The others are hollow: another place fits their routes almost as well.
mesh.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: a plane that fits the flight times as well as the sphere, or a sphere whose airports land far from their real places.
fx-mesh.title: The plane and the sphere differ by one number
fx-mesh.mini: Each route's time = climb and descent + its length. On a plane the length is the straight line; on a sphere it is the arc R ω, with R free: a very large sphere is the plane again.
fx-mesh.text: Each round trip's airborne time is the time spent climbing and descending plus the route's length, measured in hours of flight [1]. On a plane the length is the straight line between the two airports, wherever they are put. On a sphere it is the arc R ω, ω being the angle between the airports seen from the centre and R the sphere's radius, also free. Two numbers per airport on both surfaces, and one more for the sphere, its size; a sphere large enough is a plane, so the plane is one of the sphere's choices.
fx-mesh.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: flight times for which the best radius is infinite, the plane itself.
